q: Which is the main indication for awake craniotomy?
o: Resection near eloquent cortex (speech or motor)
why: Awake testing allows maximal safe resection near eloquent areas; it is also used for epilepsy surgery and DBS.

q: Which is an absolute contraindication to awake craniotomy?
o: Raised ICP or inability to lie still and cooperate
why: Absolute: patient refusal, inability to cooperate or lie still, raised ICP.

q: Which nerve is NOT included in a scalp block?
why: The 7 nerves: supraorbital, supratrochlear, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal, greater auricular, greater occipital, lesser occipital.

q: During cortical mapping, the patient has a focal seizure. What is the first treatment?
o: Ask the surgeon to irrigate the cortex with ice-cold saline
why: Ice-cold saline on the brain surface usually stops it; small doses of propofol or midazolam if needed (they suppress the ECoG).

q: What is an advantage of dexmedetomidine for awake craniotomy?
o: It is a good analgesic alone
why: Dexmedetomidine (alpha-2 agonist, about 8× more selective than clonidine) sedates with little respiratory depression; it can cause bradycardia and hypotension.

q: What is the main airway risk during the asleep phase of an asleep–awake–asleep technique?
o: Airway obstruction and hypoventilation with limited head access
why: The head is fixed in pins; have an LMA ready and a plan for airway rescue.

q: What is the definition of status epilepticus used for treatment?
o: A seizure over 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery
why: Treat seizures lasting over 5 minutes; long-term harm is more likely after about 30 minutes.

q: What is the first-line treatment for status epilepticus in hospital?
o: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (e.g. 4 mg), repeated once
why: First line is a benzodiazepine; second line levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate; third line GA or phenobarbital.

q: Which second-line drug is given as 60 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes for status epilepticus?
why: Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g); phenytoin 15–18 mg/kg; valproate 40 mg/kg.

q: What happens after about 60 minutes of continuous seizure activity?
o: Decompensation: hypotension, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, rhabdomyolysis and cerebral oedema
why: Autoregulation fails, with acidosis, hyperkalaemia, rhabdomyolysis and neuronal death.
